t: The Wording Game — Greedy Simulation with Two Pointers
o: Alice is forced to open with her smallest word a[0]. Thereafter, whoever cannot play a closely-greater word loses. Playing the SMALLEST legal word is optimal: it keeps your larger options available while restricting the opponent as little as necessary in terms of your own future flexibility — the standard exchange argument shows passing up a smaller playable word never helps. So the game reduces to a two-pointer simulation: each turn, advance the mover's pointer past words that aren't closely greater than the last played word; if the pointer runs off the end, the mover loses. Example 1: Alice plays "avokado", Bob plays "brazil", Alice has nothing starting with 'b'/'c' greater → false.
k: Greedy: always play your smallest closely-greater word; simulate with two pointers over the sorted lists.

a.i: Keep pointers ia (starting at 1, since a[0] is played) and ib. On Bob's turn, skip b[j] while it is not closely greater than last; if exhausted Bob loses; otherwise play it and advance. Mirror for Alice. Return whether Alice wins.
s: Play last = a[0], mover = Bob, ia = 1, ib = 0.
While true: advance the mover's pointer past words failing closelyGreater(word, last).
If the pointer is exhausted, the mover loses (return accordingly).
Otherwise set last = that word, advance the pointer, swap the mover.
a.t: O(|a| + |b|) pointer advances — each word is skipped at most once; comparisons cost O(word length)

w: State the greedy-exchange argument explicitly in an interview: holding back a bigger word only delays using it and hands the opponent the same position or better. Pitfalls: forgetting Alice MUST open with a[0] (not a choice), the closely-greater first-letter rule (same letter or exactly one letter ahead), and returning the winner relative to who failed to move. Total word-length bound (10^6) keeps string comparisons cheap.
